editorial.headline: Bread, Biscuits and Cakes: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This specialist retail activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet PMA registration in Bali is blocked under the province-wide moratorium.
editorial.body:
This activity covers specialist retail sales of breads, dry cakes and wet cakes: sweet breads, loaf bread, sponge cakes, cakes, tarts, biscuits, wafers, semprong, cookies and related products. Its centre of gravity is the retail counter and the customer-facing sale of these bakery and confectionery items, rather than a broad statement about food commerce. For a founder, that distinction matters because the registered activity is defined by this particular retail assortment.

The activity is open at every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That makes the code usable across a wide range of business sizes, from the smallest category through to a large enterprise. The national investment position is equally clear. It is classified as open, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In national terms, foreign investment is therefore permitted without a stated foreign-equity cap below full ownership.

Bali presents a materially different registration picture for PMA. In Bali today, this activity cannot be registered as PMA by a foreigner. At the Besar scale, OSS assigns Low or Medium-Low risk across every scope of the activity, placing it within Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium on all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA. The restriction is not a national foreign-ownership limit recast in local language; nationally the activity remains open to 100% foreign ownership. It is a Bali-specific block on PMA registration arising from the provincial moratorium and the activity’s stated risk position.

That leaves a straightforward but consequential reading. The national framework says this specialist retail business is open to foreign ownership at all listed scales. The Bali framework says PMA registration is blocked, because the relevant risk classifications fall within the provincial moratorium. Founders considering this activity should treat those as two distinct facts that must both be true in the place where the business is to be registered: national openness establishes the general investment position, while Bali’s moratorium determines the local PMA registration outcome.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally this specialist retail activity is open to 100% foreign ownership, but Bali blocks its PMA registration under the province-wide moratorium.
